transcript:
Meeting Header:
- Date: 2026-05-15
- Time: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Sara Gomez (PM), Arjun Rao (ML Eng), Tom Li (DevOps)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood walkthrough of hosted chat generation, streaming demo with retries, parameter tuning. Discussed VPC/private deployments, KMS, SOC 2; asked about latency SLOs and cost targets. Next step: send security docs and run a short POC.

Topics: Streaming responses, generation params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry patterns and exponential backoff, Console quick tour, Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching and caching), private/VPC and KMS, benchmarking.

Transcript Body:
[00:00:05] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, appreciate it. Quick intros — I'm Maya, AE, and Liam here is our solutions engineer.
[00:00:12] Liam: Hey all, hi, super. we'll do a quick product tour then a demo, then leave time for questions.
[00:00:20] Sara: Sounds good, we have about 40 minutes, and then Tom needs to run.
[00:00:25] Maya: Perfect. BrightData — quick context, Sara, you said you care about sub-200ms p50 for simple prompt flows and cost at scale, right?
[00:00:35] Sara: Yeah, that's right. For our agent UI the response latency target is 200-300ms p50 p95 we'd like lower but 300ms is max during peak. Also we need SOC2 and VPC options.
[00:00:46] Liam: Got it. We'll show streaming which helps perceived latency, then talk about routing and fallbacks if a model variant is slower.
[00:00:53] Maya: Quick agenda — demo of hosted chat endpoint, parameters (temp, top_p, max_tokens), streaming behavior, retries/backoff patterns, and quick Console + Optimize tips.

[00:01:12] Liam: Alright I'm switching to the browser, forgive my tabs. So here's the Redwood Console — model catalog on the left; for hosted the default is our curated open models or Redwood-verified ones.
[00:01:28] Liam: I'll call the chat endpoint with streaming. Note: streaming is chunked server-sent events; in our SDK you get a callback per delta token so UI can render progressively.
[00:01:44] [Demo typing noise]
[00:01:50] Liam: Sending a sample prompt: "Summarize the following blob for an analyst" — you'll see tokens stream in.
[00:02:05] Arjun: Quick question — streaming does that still count tokens in the same billing unit as usual?
[00:02:12] Maya: Yes, pricing is per generated token; streaming is just delivery. You still pay for generated tokens the same way.
[00:02:20] Tom: And can we switch off streaming? We have some clients that prefer full response only.
[00:02:26] Liam: Yes you can, you can request non-streaming in the call and get the whole payload. Streaming is optional.

[00:02:45] Liam: Okay demo: you'll notice initial prefix tokens sometimes cached — we do prefix/K V cache, sorry K V — KV cache for repeated prompts to speed up multipass.
[00:02:58] Sara: Can you explain KV cache a bit more?
[00:03:03] Liam: Sure. If you have a repeated system prompt or context that overlaps, KV cache avoids recomputing earlier layers which reduces latency and GPU compute. It helps latency and cost.

[00:03:28] Liam: Now parameters: temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling; max_tokens obviously caps. Also we expose top_k and repetition penalties.
[00:03:39] Arjun: For our throughput we typically run high QPS with short outputs — 20 tokens avg. What parameter sets generally keep latency low?
[00:03:48] Liam: Lower temperature and lower max_tokens helps. Also reduce sequence length by trimming context. For short outputs batching is helpful, but batching trades latency for throughput. In hosted mode we have workload-aware batching that tries to honor latency SLOs.

[00:04:10] Sara: How aggressive is that batching? I want to avoid p95 spikes.
[00:04:15] Liam: You can configure latency SLO per route; Redwood's runtime will limit batch window to meet the SLO. If you're on Dedicated you can set stricter guarantees.

[00:04:35] Maya: On retries — we recommend exponential backoff with jitter for transient 5xx or 429s. Our SDK has built-in retry middleware that implements backoff and can be tuned.
[00:04:47] Tom: Do retries count as extra tokens or requests for billing?
[00:04:52] Maya: Retries re-run the request, so if the retry succeeds and generates tokens, those are billed. For transient failures where server didn't generate tokens, there's no token billing.

[00:05:10] Liam: Doing a small simulated failure — you can configure fast failover to a cheaper model variant if a higher tier hits capacity. We show fallbacks in the Console rollout policy UI.
[00:05:25] Sara: If we failover to a quantized variant, will responses change quality?
[00:05:30] Liam: Possibly slightly, but we recommend A/B testing. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles per workload based on evals.

[00:06:05] Arjun: About the SDK, do you have a node client? We use Node + Go microservices.
[00:06:11] Maya: Yes official SDKs for Node, Python, and Go. Also simple REST if you want to integrate directly.

[00:06:30] Liam: I want to show param tuning quickly — here's a sample request with temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9, max_tokens=32. Watch the stream: small deltas, quick finish.
[00:06:45] [stream chunks appear]
[00:06:53] Sara: That looks pretty snappy. What's the p50 for this model in your benchmarks?
[00:06:58] Liam: On our hosted tier this model is typically 120-180ms p50 for 20-token outputs in our us-east region, depending on load. p95 is higher and depends on batching and kernel selection.

[00:07:18] Tom: How do we measure in our environment? We want to run comparable tests.
[00:07:23] Maya: We'll provide a benchmark harness. Liam will share a script to replay representative traffic and measure latency/cost.

[00:07:40] Sara: Security questions: we require SSO, SAML, audit logs, and KMS for keys. Also data residency in EU for some customers.
[00:07:51] Liam: We support SAML SSO and RBAC. Audit logs are in Console and can be exported. For key management, we integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments; hosted can do envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key is available for Dedicated/Private.
[00:08:07] Liam: For EU residency we have region routing; you can pin requests to EU region endpoints.

[00:08:25] Sara: If we go hosted, are logs persisted forever?
[00:08:29] Maya: By default logs are retained for 30 days; enterprise plans can extend retention and we also have options to forward logs to your logging sink via syslog or S3.

[00:08:45] Arjun: For on-prem or air-gapped, is the runtime identical?
[00:08:49] Liam: Yes, the runtime is the same; the difference is control plane. Some kernel optimizations depend on GPU drivers but functionally it's equivalent. There may be slight perf differences based on hardware.

[00:09:10] Maya: Back to retries — practical pattern: use short initial timeout, then 3 retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and detect idempotency by request IDs for multi-step workflows.

[00:09:28] Sara: Any recommendations for UI to show partial streaming tokens while retries happen? We worry about flicker.
[00:09:33] Liam: Show progressive text and on retry append a note if you re-started generation; ideally do a client-side dedupe if you detect repeated prefixes. Also use server provided request_id to correlate.

[00:09:55] Liam: Now quick Console tour: route configs, per-route SLOs, and SDK keys. Here's the analytic view with token usage by route.
[00:10:10] [screen share noise]
[00:10:18] Liam: You can see token breakdown by prompt vs. generated — helps debug cost.
[00:10:26] Arjun: Nice. Do you expose per-token latencies?
[00:10:30] Liam: We have token-level histograms per model and per route — useful for heavy tail analysis.

[00:10:50] Maya: Now a couple Optimize tips: enable prefix caching for repeated system prompts, enable KV cache where possible, and consider quantization with eval-driven checks. For short-response UIs, choose smaller model width and tune max_tokens.

[00:11:18] Sara: Quantization concerns — will that break hallucination profiles?
[00:11:22] Liam: Sometimes quantization can change behavior slightly; we recommend running your eval suites against quantized variants. Redwood Optimize automates eval comparisons and will alert on regressions.

[00:11:45] Tom: For Dedicated capacity, what's the billing model and commit?
[00:11:50] Maya: Dedicated is a reserved-capacity contract with monthly commit for GPUs. There's a base fee plus token/compute unit pricing; we'll send a tailored estimate.

[00:12:10] Sara: If we start with hosted and then want to move to Dedicated, is the rollout seamless?
[00:12:16] Liam: Yes, same API and Console. You can pin rollout policies to Dedicated pools and do canary traffic.

[00:12:35] [00:12:35] Arjun: Are there any quotas for concurrent streams? We need ~200 concurrent users during spikes.
[00:12:42] Liam: For hosted we have soft limits; we can increase with plan upgrades. For Dedicated you own the capacity. We'll estimate based on tokens-per-second.

[00:13:03] Sara: Any gotchas with web sockets vs SSE streaming?
[00:13:08] Liam: SSE is reliable and simple for most browsers. WebSocket gives two-way but often adds complexity; we support both at the infra level.

[00:13:28] Maya: Okay let's show a failure scenario and how the SDK handles it. Liam?
[00:13:33] Liam: Simulating a 429. SDK does 3 retries with backoff and returns an aggregated error if fails. If a retry is successful, you just get the token stream — no partial double billing.

[00:13:55] Tom: Clarify "no double billing" — earlier you said retries that generate tokens are billed.
[00:14:00] Liam: Right — if a retry makes the server generate tokens, they are billed. What I mean is aborted partial streams where server didn't finalize means no billing. If you want guaranteed-once semantics, use idempotency keys and server-side dedupe logic.

[00:14:25] Sara: Let's talk about observability — can we hook traces into our APM?
[00:14:30] Liam: Yes, we emit traces and you can forward spans to your APM. We support distributed tracing headers so you can correlate requests end-to-end.

[00:14:50] Arjun: On the model side, do you support reranking/embeddings in the same API?
[00:14:55] Maya: Yes, we have generation, chat, embeddings and reranking endpoints. Often you combine embeddings for retrieval and then pass a condensed context to chat.

[00:15:12] Sara: Going back to cost — curious about batching effects. If we enable batching, what happens to user-perceived latency?
[00:15:18] Liam: Batching groups requests to increase GPU efficiency; that adds a small window (10-50ms typical) but increases throughput and reduces per-token cost. Redwood's batching is workload-aware and attempts to keep within configured SLOs.

[00:15:38] Maya: Quick note — Optimize will surface recommendations: e.g., reduce sequence length, enable prefix cache, or target a quantized variant with X% lower tokens cost.

[00:15:55] Sara: Great. Can you share that Optimize report sample?
[00:15:59] Maya: Yes we'll attach a sample Optimize report.

[00:16:10] [Demo continues — small prompts and streaming responses]
[00:16:40] Arjun: For the POC, we'll need the benchmark harness and expected dataset.
[00:16:45] Maya: We'll include the harness and a sample JMeter-style script and a replay tool.

[00:17:05] Tom: Ops question — network egress and peering, we prefer VPC peering.
[00:17:10] Liam: For Private and Dedicated we support VPC peering and private endpoints. For hosted we can do private networking via partner links but dedicated/private are recommended for strict network controls.

[00:17:28] Sara: Any SLA numbers?
[00:17:31] Maya: Hosted has best-effort with SLOs published; Dedicated comes with SLA for uptime and latency tiers. We'll include SLA docs.

[00:17:50] Arjun: A couple of edge questions: token truncation behavior, and how is partial output handled in retries?
[00:17:58] Liam: If you hit max_tokens we return a truncation flag in the response metadata. For retries, the SDK can be configured to resume or restart generation; resume requires stateful requests and is easier on Dedicated/private where KV persistence is controlled by you.

[00:18:25] Sara: This is super helpful. Any concerns about legal/procurement? We have standard data processing addendum and vendor security questionnaires.
[00:18:33] Maya: We handle DPAs and can go through procurement. For legal questionnaires we'll have security provide answers; I'll route that.

[00:18:50] [Longer demo sequence — some background typing, short pauses]
[00:19:30] Liam: Final piece — configuration in the Console for automatic fallbacks: you can route by policy (latency, cost, region) and fallback to model variants.

[00:19:50] Sara: We'll likely want cost caps and automatic fallback to cheaper variants when budget triggers.
[00:19:55] Liam: Yep, you can set budget triggers and automated rollback.

[00:20:10] Maya: Quick recap and next steps: we'll send security docs (SOC2 + KMS notes), Liam shares quickstart and benchmark harness, pricing + Dedicated estimate, and schedule the POC kickoff week of 5/25.
[00:20:26] Sara: Sounds good, thanks.
[00:20:30] Arjun: Thanks, that works for engineering.
[00:20:33] Tom: Thanks, I'll follow up with network details.
[00:20:36] Maya: Awesome. Any last Qs?
[00:20:39] Sara: None from me.
[00:20:40] Maya: Great, we'll send notes and attach links. Thanks everyone.
[00:20:45] Liam: Bye.
